title.text: Jumalon Museum, Butterfly Sanctuary and Art Gallery

title_en.text: Jumalon Museum, Butterfly Sanctuary and Art Gallery

tagline.text: Hidden in Basak Pardo: the Philippines' oldest butterfly garden and wing-mosaic gallery

location.label: Location
location.text: Julian N. Jumalon Street (formerly Macopa Street), Basak Pardo, Cebu City

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May dry season (butterflies are most active on bright, warm days)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–500 (per person, admission and transport, rough estimate)

children.text: The Jumalon Museum, Butterfly Sanctuary and Art Gallery is a private facility in Basak Pardo, Cebu City, that has opened a former family home as a butterfly museum, garden and art gallery since 1974. You can see butterfly specimens, a garden of about 100 butterfly food plant species, and mosaics made from butterfly wings in one place.

The Jumalon Museum, Butterfly Sanctuary and Art Gallery is a small private museum tucked into a residential neighborhood in Basak Pardo, in southern Cebu City. Julian Navarro Jumalon (born 1909), a Cebuano lepidopterist and painter, turned his own home into a butterfly museum, garden and gallery in 1974, and today the Jumalon Foundation, set up by his descendants, looks after the collection and grounds. Wikipedia describes the collection as the oldest, and perhaps the biggest, butterfly collection in the Philippines. It is not as large or showy as the Basilica del Santo Niño or Magellan's Cross, but few places in the city let you enjoy butterflies and art together in such a quiet setting.

What makes the place special is that three things share one compound. The first is the museum, which holds specimens of butterflies, moths, beetles and other insects. It includes butterflies collected in the Philippines as well as specimens from around the world, with notes on the ecology of each kind. The second is the garden, planted with about 100 species of butterfly food plants. Jumalon cultivated food plants in his yard so butterflies would come on their own, and the garden is said to attract about 50 local and foreign butterfly species. Some rare species are reportedly hatched in captivity and then released into the garden. The third is the gallery of Julian Jumalon's paintings and lepido mosaics.

Lepido mosaics are the art form that made this place famous. Jumalon collected butterfly wings that collectors had discarded as damaged, sent to him by mail from all over the world. He then cut them into very thin slivers with a scalpel and tweezers and glued them together to form people and landscapes. The pieces showing Cebu City landmarks and national heroes are said to be the most popular. No paint is used, yet the blues, emerald greens, golds and blacks come from the wings themselves, and up close they look quite different from photos. One visitor reported that photography is not allowed inside the gallery, so please ask the staff at the entrance first.

A short visit of one to one and a half hours is enough. A guide walks with you, explains the specimens and mosaics, and answers questions, so prepare a few simple questions in English to get more out of it. It suits children well and fits into a half-day plan together with Cebu City sightseeing. However, it is an older building and a small private facility, and the condition of the facilities, the opening hours and the fees differ from source to source. We recommend checking the latest information before you go.

blocks.title: The oldest butterfly collection in the Philippines

children.text: Specimens of butterflies and other insects, gathered through Julian Jumalon's travels and exchanges with collectors overseas, are on display. Wikipedia describes it as the oldest and perhaps the biggest butterfly collection in the Philippines. You can compare everything from the most colorful species to the largest ones at a glance.

blocks.title: A butterfly garden with about 100 food plant species

children.text: The garden is planted with about 100 species of plants that butterfly larvae and adults feed on, and it is said to draw about 50 local and foreign butterfly species. How many species you see at a time varies a great deal with the weather and time of day, and some visitors report seeing only a few butterflies. A warm, sunny daytime visit is best.

You can see mosaics made by cutting up discarded butterfly wings and gluing them together. Works showing Cebu City landmarks and national heroes are the best known, and the amazing part is that the colors are the wings' own rather than paint.

Jumalon was both a lepidopterist and a painter, and his paintings are on display. One visitor account says he also took part in designing old Philippine banknotes, but we could not confirm this from another source, so we suggest asking the guide on site.

Because the place is small, a guide goes around with you explaining the butterfly species and how the works were made. One visitor wrote that the guide answered questions kindly, and another mentioned a moment of making a wish and releasing a white butterfly, though it is not confirmed whether this is a regular program.

blocks.title: A quiet retreat in the city

children.text: It sits in a residential area in the south of Cebu City, with an atmosphere completely different from the busy shopping malls or the church district. Walking slowly through the garden and waiting for butterflies is part of the charm, and the place suits patient observers better than people in a hurry to take photos.

According to a blog, you can order live butterflies for events such as weddings (as of a December 2016 visit, about ₱30 each, a minimum of 30, ordered a few days ahead). Few travelers will need this, but it shows that the place raises butterflies.

items.title: Half-day itinerary
items.subtitle: Combining Cebu City sights with Jumalon

children.text: Leave your hotel and arrive in Basak Pardo after about
20–40 minutes
. Since sources list opening hours as
, going in the morning is the relaxed choice.
Pay the admission fee at the entrance and meet your guide. Start slowly with the butterfly and insect specimens in the museum building.
Walk through the gallery with the lepido mosaics and paintings. Ask first whether photography is allowed.
Step out into the garden and watch butterflies among the food plants. They become more active as the sun gets higher.
Head back to the city for lunch, then continue in the afternoon toward the Basilica del Santo Niño and Magellan's Cross.
Basak Pardo is in a different direction from central Cebu City, so allow plenty of travel time if you combine it with the city's church district on the same day.
Arrive before it gets too hot and explore the garden first. Ask your child to find the plants where butterflies land.
In the museum, look at the specimens and explain the difference between a chrysalis and a caterpillar.
Ask the guide about the life cycle of one butterfly species. It helps to prepare one or two questions in English beforehand.
It is best not to stay too long. The place is small, so an hour and a half is enough.
A direct flight from Manila (MNL) to Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB) takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
. Check the airline's latest schedule for routes and times.
The airport is on Mactan Island, so you reach Basak Pardo by taxi or Grab, and the travel time varies greatly with traffic, so leave some margin.
One suggested way is to take a jeepney marked "Bacalso" from the city center and walk from the nearest stop to Julian N. Jumalon Street. Guides mention about
15–20 minutes
, but routes can change, so ask the driver or locals on site.
If you travel by jeepney, one visitor says the approach via Macopa Street has more shade and plenty of people to ask for directions.
This is the easiest option. Enter "Jumalon Butterfly Sanctuary, Basak Pardo" as the destination and add that it is behind Basak High School to make it easier to find.
It can be hard to catch a taxi on the way back, so set up the Grab app in advance.

Butterflies are most active on sunny, warm days at midday. The guide said there is no fixed best date, and one visitor guessed there may be more butterflies in summer (the dry season). We therefore recommend a clear morning in the dry season, December to May.
In the rainy season butterflies hardly fly when it rains, so the garden is less rewarding. The museum and gallery are indoors, though, so you can still see them in the rain.

The area around the museum is residential, with few hotels and restaurants. Most travelers stay in central Cebu City (around IT Park, Colon Street and Magellan's Cross) or on Mactan Island and visit as a day trip. The city offers a wide range of food, from Filipino to Korean restaurants, so the easiest plan is to return to the city for a meal after the museum.
There is no confirmed information about food near the entrance, so bring drinking water and a hat. The garden is outdoors with limited shade and gets hot at midday.
Check by phone or email whether it is open and what the admission fee is before you go. The contacts listed in a 2017 blog are (32) 261-6884 or 0921-441-8491, but they may have changed.
One visitor says butterflies are attracted to sweet-scented perfume. A light scent is better than a strong smell.
Ask at the entrance first whether photography is allowed in the gallery. One visitor reports that it is prohibited.
In the garden, approach butterflies slowly while they are resting and do not catch them by hand. Their wing scales are easily damaged.
Because it is a small facility, it is better to contact them in advance for group visits. There was a separate group rate (20 or more).
Bring a hat, sunscreen and water. Going in the morning rather than midday is better for butterflies and less hot.
One visitor says the approach from the Macopa Street side is shaded and more comfortable to walk if you come by jeepney.
Fees and operating details differ from source to source, so be sure to confirm the latest information locally before visiting. Some sources also say admission is free or by donation.
Most sources list opening hours as daily
, but one source gives Monday to Saturday
. Check especially on public holidays.
Some visitors report seeing only a few butterflies in the garden. Even if you do not see many, think of the museum and gallery as the main attractions.
Taxi drivers may not know the location, so search for "Jumalon Butterfly Sanctuary" in a map app and show it to them.
Specimens and mosaics are sensitive to light and humidity, so do not touch them. Do not use a flash.
It is in a residential alley, so avoid visiting or returning late at night.
